claim: SNORD115 has been proposed to promote the activity of serotonin (HTR2C) receptor via its ability to base pair with its pre-mRNA and regulate alternative RNA splicing and/or A-to-I RNA editing.
source: SNORD115 has been proposed to promote the activity of serotonin (HTR2C) receptor via its ability to base pair with its pre-mRNA and regulate alternative RNA splicing and/or A-to-I RNA editing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature proposing this mechanism, as indicated in the introduction and discussion sections.

claim: SNORD115 genes are deleted in most patients with Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS).
source: Because SNORD115 genes are deleted in most patients with the Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS), diminished HTR2C receptor activity could contribute to the impaired emotional response and/or compulsive overeating characteristic of this disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PWS genetics referenced in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Diminished HTR2C receptor activity could contribute to the impaired emotional response and/or compulsive overeating characteristic of PWS.
source: Because SNORD115 genes are deleted in most patients with the Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS), diminished HTR2C receptor activity could contribute to the impaired emotional response and/or compulsive overeating characteristic of this disease.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: A CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Snord115 knockout mouse was created.
source: In order to test this appealing but never demonstrated hypothesis in vivo, we created a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Snord115 knockout mouse.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: Snord115 knockout mice show only modest region-specific alterations in Htr2c RNA editing profiles.
source: Surprisingly, we uncovered only modest region-specific alterations in Htr2c RNA editing profiles, while Htr2c alternative RNA splicing was unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput sequencing data presented in Figure 3 and related analyses.

claim: Htr2c alternative RNA splicing was unchanged in Snord115 knockout mice.
source: Surprisingly, we uncovered only modest region-specific alterations in Htr2c RNA editing profiles, while Htr2c alternative RNA splicing was unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR and RT-PCR data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The subtle changes in Htr2c RNA editing were not accompanied by any discernible defects in anxio-depressive-like phenotypes.
source: These subtle changes, whose functional relevance remains uncertain, were not accompanied by any discernible defects in anxio-depressive-like phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Energy balance and eating behavior were normal in Snord115 knockout mice, even after exposure to high-fat diet.
source: Energy balance and eating behavior were also normal, even after exposure to high-fat diet.
evidence: This is supported by metabolic and feeding behavior data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Box C/D small nucleolar RNAs (SNORDs) represent a well-defined family of small non-coding RNAs that exert their regulatory functions via antisense-based mechanisms.
source: Box C/D small nucleolar RNAs (SNORDs) represent a well-defined family of small non-coding RNAs that exert their regulatory functions via antisense-based mechanisms.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The vast majority of SNORDs form base-pairing interactions with ribosomal RNA (rRNA) precursor, spliceosomal U6 snRNA or tRNA and guide sequence-specific ribose methylations.
source: Indeed, the vast majority forms base-pairing interactions with ribosomal RNA (rRNA) precursor, spliceosomal U6 snRNA or tRNA and, in doing so, they guide sequence-specific ribose methylations (Cavaillé et al., 1996; Ganot et al., 1999; Kiss-László et al., 1996; Vitali and Kiss, 2019) or, in rare cases, base acetylation (Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A few SNORDs are specialized to facilitate the production of mature 18S, 28S, and 5.8S rRNA by acting as RNA folding chaperones.
source: By acting as RNA folding chaperones, a few are specialized to facilitate the production of mature 18S, 28S, and 5.8S rRNA (Watkins and Bohnsack, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Nucleoli contain orphan SNORDs lacking conserved antisense elements against canonical RNA targets.
source: Finally, nucleoli also contain orphan SNORDs lacking conserved antisense elements against canonical RNA targets, thus raising the possibility that some may interact with uncharacterized targets, possibly including mRNAs (Bratkovič et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Many orphan SNORDs are generated from two large, imprinted chromosomal domains at human 15q11q13 and 14q32.
source: Intriguingly, many orphan SNORDs are generated from two large, imprinted chromosomal domains at human 15q11q13 and 14q32 (Cavaillé, 2017; Marty and Cavaillé, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The imprinted human 15q11q13 region contains several paternally expressed, protein coding genes as well as numerous paternally expressed, neuronal-specific SNORD genes organized as two main repetitive DNA arrays: the SNORD116 and SNORD115 clusters.
source: The imprinted human 15q11q13 region - also known as the Prader-Willi Syndrome (PWS)/Angelman Syndrome (AS) locus or SNURF-SNRPN domain - contains several paternally expressed, protein coding genes as well as numerous paternally expressed, neuronal-specific SNORD genes organized as two main repetitive DNA arrays: the SNORD116 and SNORD115 clusters composed of 29 and 47 related gene copies, respectively (Cavaillé et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The SNORD116 cluster is composed of 29 related gene copies.
source: The imprinted human 15q11q13 region - also known as the Prader-Willi Syndrome (PWS)/Angelman Syndrome (AS) locus or SNURF-SNRPN domain - contains several paternally expressed, protein coding genes as well as numerous paternally expressed, neuronal-specific SNORD genes organized as two main repetitive DNA arrays: the SNORD116 and SNORD115 clusters composed of 29 and 47 related gene copies, respectively (Cavaillé et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The SNORD115 cluster is composed of 47 related gene copies.
source: The imprinted human 15q11q13 region - also known as the Prader-Willi Syndrome (PWS)/Angelman Syndrome (AS) locus or SNURF-SNRPN domain - contains several paternally expressed, protein coding genes as well as numerous paternally expressed, neuronal-specific SNORD genes organized as two main repetitive DNA arrays: the SNORD116 and SNORD115 clusters composed of 29 and 47 related gene copies, respectively (Cavaillé et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The lack of expression of one (or several) paternally expressed gene(s) on 15q11q13 is genetically linked to Prader Willi Syndrome.
source: The lack of expression of one (or several) paternally expressed gene(s) on 15q11q13 is genetically linked to Prader Willi Syndrome (Buiting, 2010; Cassidy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PWS is characterized by poor feeding and muscular hypotonia in the perinatal period.
source: This rare human genetic disorder is characterized by poor feeding and muscular hypotonia in the perinatal period while, in the childhood and adulthood, individuals with PWS manifest an obsession with food and eating that, if not controlled, leads to life-threatening obesity.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about PWS.

claim: In childhood and adulthood, individuals with PWS manifest an obsession with food and eating that, if not controlled, leads to life-threatening obesity.
source: This rare human genetic disorder is characterized by poor feeding and muscular hypotonia in the perinatal period while, in the childhood and adulthood, individuals with PWS manifest an obsession with food and eating that, if not controlled, leads to life-threatening obesity.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about PWS.

claim: PWS symptoms include decreased energy expenditure, growth delay, abnormalities in hormonal profiles, hypogonadism, dysfunction of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, respiratory problems, high pain threshold, sleep disturbance, learning disabilities as well as diverse psychopathological issues.
source: Other symptoms include decreased energy expenditure, growth delay, abnormalities in hormonal profiles, hypogonadism, dysfunction of the hypothalamus-pituitary axis, respiratory problems, high pain threshold, sleep disturbance, learning disabilities as well as diverse psychopathological issues notably in terms of obsessive-compulsive behavior and anxio-depressive traits (Butler et al., 2019; Cassidy et al., 2012; Muscogiuri et al., 2019; Thuilleaux et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about PWS supported by citations.

claim: Deficiencies in SNORDs have recently emerged as one of the key determinants for PWS.
source: Although the genotype-phenotype relationship in PWS is complex and not entirely understood, deficiencies in SNORDs have recently emerged as one of the key determinants for the disease.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature on PWS genetics.

claim: Rare PWS individuals bear ~71–200 kb-long paternally inherited deletions overlapping the SNORD gene array, particularly SNORD116 genes.
source: This is evidenced by rare PWS individuals bearing ~71–200 kb-long paternally inherited deletions overlapping the SNORD gene array, particularly SNORD116 genes (Bieth et al., 2015; de Smith et al., 2009; Duker et al., 2010; Fontana et al., 2017; Sahoo et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to case reports and genetic studies.

claim: Snord116-deficient mice are growth-retarded and show increased food intake.
source: Remarkably, Snord116-deficient mice are growth-retarded and show increased food intake, two abnormalities reminiscent of PWS phenotype (Ding et al., 2008; Skryabin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior mouse model studies.

claim: The relevance of increased food intake with respect to the lower body weight of Snord116 mutants was recently questioned.
source: The relevance of increased food intake with respect to the lower body weight of Snord116 mutants was, however, recently questioned (Polex-Wolf et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Loss of Snord116 is not accompanied by any signs of obesity.
source: Importantly, loss of Snord116 is not accompanied by any signs of obesity and, paradoxically, Snord116-deficient mice appear even protected from high fat-diet induced obesity (Ding et al., 2008; Qi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Snord116-deficient mice appear protected from high fat-diet induced obesity.
source: Importantly, loss of Snord116 is not accompanied by any signs of obesity and, paradoxically, Snord116-deficient mice appear even protected from high fat-diet induced obesity (Ding et al., 2008; Qi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Snord116-KO mice do not fully recapitulate the entire set of PWS phenotypes.
source: Thus, Snord116-KO mice, like all other PWS mouse models, do not fully recapitulate the entire set of PWS phenotypes (Bervini and Herzog, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference from the described phenotypes.

claim: Adult mice bearing a constitutive inactivation of the Htr2c gene are hyperphagic and overweight.
source: First, adult mice bearing a constitutive inactivation of the Htr2c gene are hyperphagic and overweight (Nonogaki et al., 1998; Tecott et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Increased food intake and growth retardation were reported in knock-in mice that only produce the fully edited (VGV), less active HTR2C isoform.
source: Second, increased food intake and growth retardation were reported in knock-in mice that only produce the fully edited (VGV), less active HTR2C isoform (Kawahara et al., 2008; Morabito et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Induced changes in Htr2c alternative splicing patterns mediated by antisense oligonucleotides alter food intake in mice.
source: Third, induced changes in Htr2c alternative splicing patterns mediated by antisense oligonucleotides alter food intake in mice (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Defects in HTR2C pathways, including altered RNA editing, are involved in the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders, particularly anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive behaviors, and schizophrenia.
source: Fourth, defects in HTR2C pathways, including altered RNA editing, are involved in the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders, particularly anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive behaviors, and schizophrenia (Chagraoui et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Defects in Htr2c-related behaviors were described in the PWS-IC mouse model.
source: Fifth, and perhaps even more tellingly, defects in Htr2c-related behaviors were described in the PWS-IC mouse model in which all paternally inherited alleles in the cluster are silenced (Davies et al., 2019; Doe et al., 2009; Garfield et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The loss of SNORD115 is unlikely to be sufficient to elicit PWS.
source: Altogether, defective post-transcriptional processing of HTR2C pre-mRNA - and thus impaired HTR2C pathway - has been surmised to account for overeating and anxio-depressive phenotypes frequently encountered in PWS patients (Cavaillé, 2017; Stamm et al., 2017), although the loss of SNORD115 is unlikely to be sufficient to elicit PWS (Bürger et al., 2002; Runte et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Direct proofs supporting the SNORD115/HTR2C axis are still lacking at the organism level.
source: This model was first proposed 20 years ago, and it constitutes certainly the most convincing example advocating for an involvement of SNORD in modifying a protein-coding transcript (Cavaillé et al., 2000). Yet, direct proofs supporting this appealing SNORD115/HTR2C axis are still lacking at the organism level (Cavaillé, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on review of the literature.

claim: Snord115 is processed from repeated, regularly spaced introns of a poorly characterized noncoding RNA host-gene transcript.
source: Snord115 is processed from repeated, regularly spaced introns of a poorly characterized noncoding RNA host-gene transcript (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic in Figure 1A and established knowledge.

claim: Snord115 sequences are the only conserved DNA segments in placental mammals.
source: Snord115 sequences are the only conserved DNA segments in placental mammals, strongly arguing that this atypical transcription unit encodes functional small RNA species under selective pressure (Cavaillé et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Snord115 genes are only expressed from the paternal allele.
source: Because Snord115 genes are only expressed from the paternal allele, ~50% of Snord115-deficient mice are expected to be obtained in the progeny after crossing wild-type females with heterozygous males.
evidence: This is established knowledge about genomic imprinting at this locus.

claim: The Snord115 gene array is no longer expressed upon a paternally inherited deletion.
source: Indeed, the Snord115 gene array is no longer expressed upon a paternally inherited deletion while, as expected, its expression remains unaffected upon maternal transmission of the deletion (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data in Figure 1C.

claim: Snord115 expression remains unaffected upon maternal transmission of the deletion.
source: Indeed, the Snord115 gene array is no longer expressed upon a paternally inherited deletion while, as expected, its expression remains unaffected upon maternal transmission of the deletion (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data in Figure 1C.

claim: Snord115 expression was undetectable by RT-qPCR in several manually-dissected brain structures from adult mice bearing a paternally-inherited deletion.
source: Moreover, we were also unable to detect Snord115 expression by RT-qPCR in several manually-dissected brain structures from adult mice bearing a paternally-inherited deletion (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1D.

claim: The removal of Snord115 genes does not significantly alter the expression of the neighboring imprinted genes.
source: Importantly, the removal of Snord115 genes does not significantly alter the expression of the neighboring imprinted genes (Figure 1E), including that of the anti-Ube3a transcript thought to silence the paternal Ube3a allele in cis (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1E and RNA-seq data in Figure 1F.

claim: The removal of Snord115 genes does not alter the expression of the anti-Ube3a transcript.
source: Importantly, the removal of Snord115 genes does not significantly alter the expression of the neighboring imprinted genes (Figure 1E), including that of the anti-Ube3a transcript thought to silence the paternal Ube3a allele in cis (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Snord115-deficient mice are seemingly normal and progeny was obtained at expected Mendelian and sex ratios.
source: Snord115-deficient mice are seemingly normal and progeny was obtained at expected Mendelian and sex ratios, leaving unlikely any developmental defect and/or perinatal lethality.
evidence: This is based on observational data from breeding experiments.

claim: Snord115 is a massively-expressed, neuronal-specific SNORD that stably associates with the 2'-O-methyltransferase Fibrillarin in vivo and accumulates in the nucleolus.
source: Snord115 is a massively-expressed, neuronal-specific SNORD that stably associates with the 2'-O-methyltransferase Fibrillarin in vivo and accumulates in the nucleolus (Bortolin-Cavaillé and Cavaillé, 2012; Cavaillé et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Snord115 lacks an antisense element that can guide Fibrillarin to rRNA targets.
source: Yet, it lacks an antisense element that can guide Fibrillarin to rRNA targets, arguing against a direct role in specifying neuronal-specific rRNA 2'-O-methylation(s).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and established knowledge of SNORD function.

claim: A recent study failed to identify any brain-specific methylation rRNA sites.
source: In agreement with this assumption, our recent study failed to identify any brain-specific methylation rRNA sites (Hebras et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study by the same authors.

claim: The overall rRNA methylation patterns were comparable between WT and Snord115-KO brain.
source: As reported in Figure 1G, the overall rRNA methylation patterns were comparable between WT and Snord115-KO brain, with only slight changes in methylation levels at a few rRNA sites: SSU-A576, LSU-C1868, and 5.8S-U14.
evidence: This is supported by RiboMeth-seq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Only slight changes in methylation levels were observed at SSU-A576, LSU-C1868, and 5.8S-U14 in Snord115-KO brain.
source: As reported in Figure 1G, the overall rRNA methylation patterns were comparable between WT and Snord115-KO brain, with only slight changes in methylation levels at a few rRNA sites: SSU-A576, LSU-C1868, and 5.8S-U14.
evidence: This is supported by RiboMeth-seq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Methylation levels at SSU-A576, LSU-C1868, and 5.8S-U14 were unaffected in the developing (E16.5) brain of a mouse model where Snord115 and Snord116 genes are simultaneously deleted.
source: Since methylation levels at these three positions were unaffected in the developing (E16.5) brain of another mouse model where Snord115 and Snord116 genes are simultaneously deleted (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supplementary file 1), we thus conclude that neither Snord115, nor Snord116 play a prominent role in ribose methylation of rRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by RiboMeth-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither Snord115, nor Snord116 play a prominent role in ribose methylation of rRNAs.
source: Since methylation levels at these three positions were unaffected in the developing (E16.5) brain of another mouse model where Snord115 and Snord116 genes are simultaneously deleted (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supplementary file 1), we thus conclude that neither Snord115, nor Snord116 play a prominent role in ribose methylation of rRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on RiboMeth-seq data from multiple mouse models.

claim: The Htr2c pre-mRNA is alternatively spliced through the use of two 5' donor splice sites (5'-SS).
source: The Htr2c pre-mRNA is alternatively spliced through the use of two 5' donor splice sites (5'-SS) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The regular 5'-SS generates RNA2 encoding the full-length receptor.
source: The regular 5'-SS generates RNA2 encoding the full-length receptor while a cryptic 5'-SS yields an alternatively spliced transcript (RNA1) that generates a truncated, presumably non-functional receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Htr2c splicing.

claim: A cryptic 5'-SS yields an alternatively spliced transcript (RNA1) that generates a truncated, presumably non-functional receptor.
source: The regular 5'-SS generates RNA2 encoding the full-length receptor while a cryptic 5'-SS yields an alternatively spliced transcript (RNA1) that generates a truncated, presumably non-functional receptor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Htr2c splicing.

claim: The binding of Snord115 nearby the cryptic 5'-SS was proposed to favor the production of RNA2.
source: The binding of Snord115 nearby the cryptic 5'-SS was proposed to favor the production of RNA2 (Cavaillé et al., 2000; Doe et al., 2009; Garfield et al., 2016; Kishore and Stamm, 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature supported by citations.

claim: The steady state levels of Htr2c mRNAs were globally unchanged in whole brain and in eight manually-dissected brain regions of adult Snord115-deficient mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, the steady state levels of Htr2c mRNAs, as assayed by a couple of primers matching the 5'-UTR, were globally unchanged in whole brain as well as in eight manually-dissected brain regions of adult Snord115-deficient mice.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only striatum showed a significant increase in Htr2c mRNA abundance in Snord115-deficient mice.
source: Only striatum showed a significant increase in Htr2c mRNA abundance, as compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lack of Snord115 did not cause any obvious changes in the profiles of alternative splicing of Htr2c pre-mRNA, including in spinal cord.
source: We then tested the lack of Snord115 on alternative splicing of Htr2c pre-mRNA by measuring the RNA2-to-RNA1 ratio by RT-qPCR. Again, lack of Snord115 did not cause any obvious changes in the profiles of alternative splicing, including in spinal cord (Figure 2C -left).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adult hypothalamus displayed a slight increase in the RNA2-to-RNA1 ratio in Snord115-deficient mice.
source: Adult hypothalamus even displayed a slight increase in the RNA2-to-RNA1 ratio.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The increase in RNA2-to-RNA1 ratio in adult hypothalamus was not seen in another independent cohort.
source: This effect was, however, not seen in another independent cohort (not shown).
evidence: This is based on unreported experimental data.

claim: Choroid plexus showed highest RNA1 level as compared to hypothalamus.
source: As controls, and in agreement with previous findings (Canton et al., 1996), choroid plexus showed highest RNA1 level as compared to hypothalamus (Figure 2C -right), thus indicating that our RT-qPCR procedure is capable of detecting changes in the RNA2-to-RNA1 ratio.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C and citation to prior literature.

claim: Alternative splicing of hypothalamic Htr2c pre-mRNAs was unaltered in Snord115-deficient mice as demonstrated by RT-PCR analysis.
source: Finally, we demonstrated unaltered alternative splicing of hypothalamic Htr2c pre-mRNAs by RT-PCR analysis with a pair of primers that simultaneously detected RNA2 and RNA1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Htr2c pre-mRNA undergoes A-to-I RNA editing at five adenosines clustered in exon V: the A-, B-, C-, D-, and E- sites.
source: Through the action of ADAR2 and ADAR1, Htr2c pre-mRNA undergoes site-specific A-to-I RNA editing at five adenosines clustered in exon V: the A-, B-, C-, D-, and E- sites (Figure 3A -top; Burns et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Snord115 is predicted to target the C-site for 2'-O-methylation.
source: Strikingly, Snord115 is predicted to target the C-site for 2'-O-methylation (Figure 2A; Cavaillé et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on sequence complementarity analysis and citation to prior work.

claim: RNA editing of Htr2c influences HTR2C response with increased RNA editing correlating with diminished G-protein coupling efficacy and reduced constitutive activity.
source: Remarkably, RNA editing influences HTR2C response with increased RNA editing correlating with diminished G-protein coupling efficacy and reduced constitutive activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HTR2C receptor function.

claim: Editing at the C- and E-sites plays a pivotal role in modulating the HTR2C signaling pathway.
source: Of note, editing at the C- and E-sites plays a pivotal role in modulating the HTR2C signaling pathway (Berg et al., 2001; Burns et al., 1997; Fitzgerald et al., 1999; Niswender et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Introducing a 2'-O-methylation at an editing site specifically decreases ADAR-mediated deamination in vitro.
source: Given that introducing a 2'-O-methylation at an editing site specifically decreases ADAR-mediated deamination in vitro (Yi-Brunozzi et al., 1999), we logically anticipated that editing at the target C-site should increase in Snord115-deficient mice as previously proposed based on artificial, non-neuronal cell systems (Vitali et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior in vitro study.

claim: The A, B, and D sites are more edited compared to C and E sites in Htr2c mRNA.
source: Indeed, given the high sequencing coverage (~1 million reads per genotype) and the substantial number of mice analyzed (n = 8–12 per genotype), there was little inter-mouse variability, with highly similar editing patterns to those previously published: the A, B, and D sites being more edited compared to C and E sites (Abbas et al., 2010; Morabito et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput sequencing data and citations to prior studies.

claim: Editing frequencies at each of the five individual sites remained globally unaltered in Snord115-KO mice.
source: Our analyses showed that editing frequencies at each of the five individual sites remained globally unaltered in Snord115-KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A few alterations in editing frequencies at a magnitude ranging from 1 to 4% were identified, particularly in the hypothalamus, brainstem, and raphe.
source: Nevertheless, we identified a few alterations at a magnitude ranging from 1 to 4%, particularly in the hypothalamus, brainstem, and raphe (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Altered expression was observed for 44 Htr2c isoforms in Snord115-KO mice, with most (28 out of 44) corresponding to lowly expressed transcripts accounting for less than 5% of the total.
source: Regarding the relative proportions of Htr2c isoforms (Figure 3C), we observed altered expression for 44 isoforms, with most of them (28 out of 44) corresponding to lowly expressed Htr2c transcripts accounting for less than 5% of the total.
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput sequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Htr2c RNA editing increases over time, from embryogenesis to adulthood.
source: Because Htr2c RNA editing increases over time, from embryogenesis to adulthood (Wahlstedt et al., 2009), we reasoned that lack of Snord115 could be more detrimental during dynamic changes in RNA editing.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Adult tissues displayed an overall increase in editing as compared to their E16.5 counterparts.
source: As expected, adult tissues displayed an overall increase in editing as compared to their E16.5 counterparts.
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The comparison of Snord115-deficient samples with WT at E16.5 did not reveal any significant differences in editing levels at any of the five sites, except for slight increase at the B-site and a very few changes in mRNA isoforms for prefrontal cortex.
source: However, the comparison of Snord115-deficient samples with WT did not reveal any significant differences in editing levels at any of the five sites, except for slight increase at the B-site and a very few changes in mRNA isoforms for prefrontal cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Htr2c RNA editing profiles remained largely unaltered in hypothalamus of adult mice chronically treated with mCPP.
source: Finally, Htr2c RNA editing profiles also remained largely unaltered in hypothalamus of adult mice chronically treated with the preferential HTR2C agonist meta-chlorophenylpiperazine (mCPP), or even in P1 or adult hypothalamus of mice simultaneously deleted for Snord115 and Snord116 genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Htr2c RNA editing profiles remained largely unaltered in P1 or adult hypothalamus of mice simultaneously deleted for Snord115 and Snord116 genes.
source: Finally, Htr2c RNA editing profiles also remained largely unaltered in hypothalamus of adult mice chronically treated with the preferential HTR2C agonist meta-chlorophenylpiperazine (mCPP), or even in P1 or adult hypothalamus of mice simultaneously deleted for Snord115 and Snord116 genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The exploratory drive and locomotion were not altered in Snord115 mutant mice in the open field test.
source: As judged by the distance travelled (Figure 4A -left), the exploratory drive and locomotion were not altered in Snord115 mutant mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Anxiety levels of Snord115-KO mice were in the normal range in the open field test.
source: Anxiety levels of Snord115-KO mice were also in the normal range, as evidenced by the number of entries (not shown) and time spent (Figure 4A -right) in the central zone of the OF considered as anxiogenic for rodents.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The frequencies of entry and time spent in the open arms of the elevated plus maze were indistinguishable between Snord115-deficient mice and WT littermates.
source: Again, the frequencies of entry (not shown) and time spent (Figure 4B) in the open arms of Snord115-deficient mice were found indistinguishable from that of their WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Snord115-KO mice showed an increase in the latency to feed in the novelty-suppressed feeding test.
source: Interestingly, Snord115-KO mice showed an increase in the latency to feed compared to WT (Figure 4C -left).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The increased latency to feed in Snord115-KO mice cannot be attributable to change in hunger.
source: These results cannot be attributable to change in hunger since food consumption in the home cage 5 min after the test showed no differences between both groups (Figure 4C -right).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The duration of immobility in the tail suspension test was similar between Snord115-deficient mice and WT.
source: As shown in Figure 4D and E, the duration of immobility of Snord115-deficient mice were similar to that of WT.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The duration of immobility in the forced swim test was similar between Snord115-deficient mice and WT.
source: As shown in Figure 4D and E, the duration of immobility of Snord115-deficient mice were similar to that of WT.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Both WT and Snord115-deficient mice spent more time contacting a stranger mouse (S1) than an empty compartment in the three-chamber test, with no difference between the two genotypes.
source: As shown in Figure 4F -left, both WT and Snord115-deficient mice spent more time in contacting S1 with no difference between the two genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: No apparent signs of aggression were detected in Snord115-deficient mice.
source: Of note, we did not detect any apparent signs of aggression.
evidence: This is based on observational data during behavioral testing.

claim: Both WT and Snord115-deficient mice interacted more with a novel intruder (S2) than a familiar one (S1) in the three-chamber test.
source: Finally, we also tested the preference for social novelty by introducing another stranger (S2) mouse. Again, we did not find any differences between WT and KO mice with, as expected, both genotypes interacting more with the novel intruder (S2) than the familiar one (S1) (Figure 4F -right).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Social preference and recognition are unchanged in Snord115-KO mice.
source: Taken together, these observations showed that social preference and recognition are unchanged in Snord115-KO mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on behavioral test data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Snord115 is expressed in most, if not all, pro-opiomelanocortin (Pomc) neurons in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus.
source: Snord115 is expressed in most, if not all, pro-opiomelanocortin (Pomc) neurons in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus (supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data referenced in supplementary file 2.

claim: The activation of HTR2C in ARC Pomc neurons promotes satiety and regulates body weight, energy balance, and glucose homeostasis.
source: The activation of HTR2C in ARC Pomc neurons, but also in nucleus of the solitary tract, promotes satiety and it also regulates body weight, energy balance, and glucose homeostasis (Berglund et al., 2013; D'Agostino et al., 2018; Heisler et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Body weights of 8-week-old adult Snord115-KO mice were in the normal range as compared to WT littermates.
source: We found that body weights (Figure 5A) and body composition (Figure 5B) of 8-week-old adult Snord115-KO mice were in the normal range as compared to WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Body composition of 8-week-old adult Snord115-KO mice was in the normal range as compared to WT littermates.
source: We found that body weights (Figure 5A) and body composition (Figure 5B) of 8-week-old adult Snord115-KO mice were in the normal range as compared to WT littermates.
evidence: This is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Blood glucose levels were unaffected in Snord115-KO mice.
source: Moreover, blood glucose levels were also unaffected and, after a bolus administration of glucose, WT and Snord115-deficient mice displayed the same ability to regulate a glucose load (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: WT and Snord115-deficient mice displayed the same ability to regulate a glucose load.
source: Moreover, blood glucose levels were also unaffected and, after a bolus administration of glucose, WT and Snord115-deficient mice displayed the same ability to regulate a glucose load (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Both daily and nightly food intake remained unaffected in Snord115-KO mice.
source: Both daily and nightly food intake (Figure 5D), as well as physical activity (Figure 5E), remain unaffected in mutant mice while, as expected, increased food consumption and elevated locomotion during the dark phases.
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Physical activity remained unaffected in Snord115-KO mice.
source: Both daily and nightly food intake (Figure 5D), as well as physical activity (Figure 5E), remain unaffected in mutant mice while, as expected, increased food consumption and elevated locomotion during the dark phases.
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Indirect calorimetry did not detect any defect in energy expenditure in Snord115-KO mice.
source: Finally, indirect calorimetry did not detect any defect in energy expenditure (Figure 5F) or respiratory exchange ratio (RER; Figure 5G), either during daylight or at night.
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Indirect calorimetry did not detect any defect in respiratory exchange ratio (RER) in Snord115-KO mice.
source: Finally, indirect calorimetry did not detect any defect in energy expenditure (Figure 5F) or respiratory exchange ratio (RER; Figure 5G), either during daylight or at night.
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The starvation procedure led to an increase in the hypothalamic expression of the orexigenic Npy and Agrp peptide encoding mRNAs in WT mice.
source: Figure 5H shows that our starvation procedure led, as expected, to an increase in the hypothalamic expression of the orexigenic Npy and Agrp peptide encoding mRNAs in WT mice while expression of the anorexigenic Pomc peptide encoding mRNA exhibited a tendency to decrease.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Expression of the anorexigenic Pomc peptide encoding mRNA exhibited a tendency to decrease during fasting in WT mice.
source: Figure 5H shows that our starvation procedure led, as expected, to an increase in the hypothalamic expression of the orexigenic Npy and Agrp peptide encoding mRNAs in WT mice while expression of the anorexigenic Pomc peptide encoding mRNA exhibited a tendency to decrease.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Npy, Agrp, and Pomc mRNAs were roughly similarly regulated in Snord115-deficient mice during fasting.
source: Remarkably, the three above-mentioned mRNAs were roughly similarly regulated in Snord115-deficient mice during fasting.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The overall physiological response to fasting was unaffected in Snord115-deficient mice, as evidenced by body weight loss, decreased glucose levels and increased ketone level.
source: The overall physiological response to fasting was also unaffected, as evidenced by body weight loss (Figure 5I), decreased glucose levels (Figure 5J) and increased ketone level (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by metabolic data shown in Figures 5I, 5J, and 5K.

claim: mRNA-seq showed that global gene expression in hypothalamus of Snord115-deficient mice fed on regular chow diet is unaffected compared to WT.
source: Finally, mRNA-seq also showed that, in the absence of Snord115, global gene expression in hypothalamus of mice fed on regular chow diet is unaffected compared to WT.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data referenced in supplementary file 3.

claim: Only eight differentially expressed transcripts (DEG) were uncovered in hypothalamus of Snord115-deficient mice, with two of them matching the deleted genomic region.
source: Indeed, we only uncovered eight differentially expressed transcripts (DEG) with two of them matching the deleted genomic region (supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data referenced in supplementary file 3.

claim: The expression of several key appetite-related genes was in the normal range in Snord115-deficient mice.
source: Hence, the expression of several key appetite-related genes, as well as that of the neighbouring imprinted genes, was in the normal range (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: HTR2C is the main, if not the sole, target on which the preferential HTR2C agonist mCPP exerts its appetite-suppressant effects.
source: HTR2C is the main, if not the sole, target on which the preferential HTR2C agonist mCPP exerts its appetite-suppressant effects (Berglund et al., 2013; Tecott et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Food intake of NaCl-treated Snord115-deficient mice was similar to that of WT littermates.
source: Figure 5M (upper and lower panels) shows that food intake of NaCl-treated Snord115-deficient mice was similar than that of WT littermates, indicating that homeostatic feeding is normal.
evidence: This is supported by feeding behavior data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Food intake of mCPP-treated WT and Snord115-KO mice was severely and dose-dependent reduced during the first hour as compared to controls.
source: As expected, food intake of mCPP-treated WT and KO mice was severely and dose-dependent reduced during the first hour as compared to controls (50% and 90% decrease following administration of 1 and 5 mg/kg of mCPP, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by feeding behavior data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Anorectic responses of mCPP remained in the same range in both WT and Snord115-KO genotypes.
source: Given that anorectic responses of mCPP remained in the same range in both genotypes, loss of Snord115 does not perceptibly disturb the hypothalamic HTR2C signaling cascade in vivo, at least when fast-induced food intake is used as a read-out.
evidence: This is supported by feeding behavior data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Loss of Snord115 does not perceptibly disturb the hypothalamic HTR2C signaling cascade in vivo, at least when fast-induced food intake is used as a read-out.
source: Given that anorectic responses of mCPP remained in the same range in both genotypes, loss of Snord115 does not perceptibly disturb the hypothalamic HTR2C signaling cascade in vivo, at least when fast-induced food intake is used as a read-out.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on feeding behavior data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Body weight gain of Snord115-KO mice was similar to WT mice during 24 weeks of high-fat diet exposure.
source: During the course of diet-induced obesity, body weight gain of Snord115-KO mice was similar to WT mice (Figure 6A) with normal adiposity as evidenced by the weights of perigonadal, subcutaneous fat mass and liver measured after euthanasia.
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Adiposity was normal in Snord115-KO mice on high-fat diet as evidenced by the weights of perigonadal, subcutaneous fat mass and liver.
source: During the course of diet-induced obesity, body weight gain of Snord115-KO mice was similar to WT mice (Figure 6A) with normal adiposity as evidenced by the weights of perigonadal, subcutaneous fat mass and liver measured after euthanasia.
evidence: This is supported by adiposity data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Brown adipose tissue of Snord115-KO mice was 38% heavier than WT tissues after 24 weeks of high-fat diet.
source: Only brown adipose tissue showed a statistically significant change, with Snord115-KO tissues being 38% heavier than WT tissues (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by adiposity data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Capability for glucose clearance in Snord115-KO mice did not differ substantially from that of WT littermates after 12 weeks of HFD exposure.
source: Capability for glucose clearance in Snord115-KO mice did not differ substantially from that of WT littermates (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Indirect calorimetry analyses did not reveal any obvious differences in food intake between Snord115-KO and WT littermates after HFD exposure.
source: In addition, indirect calorimetry analyses did not reveal any obvious differences in food intake (Figure 6D), ambulatory activities (Figure 6E), energy expenditure (Figure 6F) or respiratory exchange ratio (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Indirect calorimetry analyses did not reveal any obvious differences in ambulatory activities between Snord115-KO and WT littermates after HFD exposure.
source: In addition, indirect calorimetry analyses did not reveal any obvious differences in food intake (Figure 6D), ambulatory activities (Figure 6E), energy expenditure (Figure 6F) or respiratory exchange ratio (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Indirect calorimetry analyses did not reveal any obvious differences in energy expenditure between Snord115-KO and WT littermates after HFD exposure.
source: In addition, indirect calorimetry analyses did not reveal any obvious differences in food intake (Figure 6D), ambulatory activities (Figure 6E), energy expenditure (Figure 6F) or respiratory exchange ratio (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Indirect calorimetry analyses did not reveal any obvious differences in respiratory exchange ratio between Snord115-KO and WT littermates after HFD exposure.
source: In addition, indirect calorimetry analyses did not reveal any obvious differences in food intake (Figure 6D), ambulatory activities (Figure 6E), energy expenditure (Figure 6F) or respiratory exchange ratio (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The study did not unveil significant metabolic differences between Snord115-KO and WT littermates after HFD exposure.
source: Altogether, our analyses did not unveil significant metabolic differences between Snord115-KO and WT littermates after HFD exposure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple metabolic measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: In vivo molecular outputs of SnoRD115/Htr2c mRNA interaction are more complex than previously inferred from in vitro observations.
source: Hence, in vivo molecular outputs of SnoRD115/Htr2c mRNA interaction are more complex than previously inferred from in vitro observations (Kishore and Stamm, 2006; Vitali et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between current in vivo findings and prior in vitro studies.

claim: Reactivation of the Snord116-Ipw-Snord115 genomic interval in choroid plexus leads to modest impact on RNA editing without any impairment in alternative splicing of Htr2c pre-mRNA.
source: Our observations are in line with two recent in vivo studies. Reactivation of the Snord116-Ipw-Snord115 genomic interval in choroid plexus - that does not normally express Snord115 - leads to modest impact on RNA editing without any impairment in alternative splicing of Htr2c pre-mRNA (Raabe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Oligonucleotides mimicking Snord115 base-pairing have no effects on alternative splicing of Htr2c pre-mRNA.
source: Moreover, oligonucleotides mimicking Snord115 base-pairing have no effects on alternative splicing, despite the fact that in vivo delivery of antisense oligonucleotides targeting other RNA segment of Htr2c pre-mRNA can alter the regular-to-truncated ratio of HTR2C (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Changes in Htr2c alternative splicing were described in the hypothalamus of PWS-IC mice.
source: Changes in Htr2c alternative splicing were described in the hypothalamus of PWS-IC mice (Garfield et al., 2016) but not in those of PWS patients studied (Bochukova et al., 2018) or in whole brain of PWS-IC mice (Doe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Changes in Htr2c alternative splicing were not found in PWS patients studied.
source: Changes in Htr2c alternative splicing were described in the hypothalamus of PWS-IC mice (Garfield et al., 2016) but not in those of PWS patients studied (Bochukova et al., 2018) or in whole brain of PWS-IC mice (Doe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Altered Htr2c RNA editing was reported in the brain of PWS-IC and PatDp/+ mouse models, but these changes did not correlate with the dosage of Snord115.
source: Third, although altered Htr2c RNA editing was reported in the brain of PWS-IC and PatDp/+ mouse models, these changes did not correlate with the dosage of Snord115 (Doe et al., 2009; Nakatani et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: No reproducible editing changes were noticed in the frontal cortex of a few PWS patients.
source: In addition, no reproducible editing changes were noticed in the frontal cortex of a few PWS patients (Glatt-Deeley et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The PWS-IC mouse model carries a paternally inherited deletion of the imprinted center (IC) region leading to the silencing of all imprinted genes positioned on the paternal allele.
source: The PWS-IC mouse model carries a paternally inherited deletion of the imprinted center (IC) region leading to the silencing of all imprinted genes positioned on the paternal allele (Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PWS-IC mouse model supported by citation.

claim: PWS-IC mice are growth retarded and it is necessary to switch to a hybrid genetic background to avoid 80–100% neonatal mortality.
source: Moreover, these knockout mice are growth retarded and it is necessary to switch to a hybrid genetic background to avoid 80–100% neonatal mortality due to absence of paternal contribution.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PWS-IC mouse model.

claim: Defects in the serotonergic system have been described in mice disrupted for the paternally expressed Magel2 gene.
source: This is all the more likely as defects in the serotonergic system have been described in mice disrupted for the paternally expressed Magel2 (Mercer et al., 2009) or Ndn (Zanella et al., 2008) genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Defects in the serotonergic system have been described in mice disrupted for the paternally expressed Ndn gene.
source: This is all the more likely as defects in the serotonergic system have been described in mice disrupted for the paternally expressed Magel2 (Mercer et al., 2009) or Ndn (Zanella et al., 2008) genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior studies.

claim: Altered expression of neuropeptide of the melanocortin system was reported in Snord116-KO mice.
source: Moreover, altered expression of neuropeptide of the melanocortin system was also reported in Snord116-KO mice (Burnett et al., 2017; Qi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Changes in the excitability of 5-HT neuronal circuitries were observed in living Snord115-KO mice.
source: As a case in point, we observed changes in the excitability of 5-HT neuronal circuitries in living Snord115-KO mice (B. Guiard, personal communication).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from a collaborator.

claim: Mice simultaneously deleted for Snord115 and Snord116 genes display more severe phenotypes than single Snord115- or Snord116-KO mice.
source: Consistent with that possibility, mice simultaneously deleted for Snord115 and Snord116 genes display more severe phenotypes than single Snord115- or Snord116-KO mice (Boursereau, Marty et al. unpublished observations).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from the authors.

claim: Transcriptomic analyses of single cells in mouse hypothalamus identified 34 neuronal cell clusters.
source: For instance, transcriptomic analyses of single cells in mouse hypothalamus identified 34 neuronal cell clusters (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Pomc neurons represent a few per cent of hypothalamic neurons with only 30–40% expressing Htr2c.
source: Pomc neurons represent a few per cent of these hypothalamic neurons with only 30–40% expressing Htr2c (Lam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Adaptive mechanisms increase the density of the fully edited (VGV) HTR2C receptor at the cell membranes, very likely compensating for its diminished activity.
source: An additional layer of complexity may also arise from poorly understood 'adaptive mechanisms' which increase the density of the fully edited (VGV) HTR2C receptor at the cell membranes, very likely compensating for its diminished activity (Kawahara et al., 2008; Morabito et al., 2010a; Olaghere da Silva et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Only rather subtle RNA editing changes were noticed with respect to genetic background or serotonin content in recent high-throughput sequencing analyses.
source: Yet, more recent high-throughput sequencing analyses did not fully confirm all these earlier findings. Only rather subtle RNA editing changes were noticed with respect to genetic background or serotonin content (Abbas et al., 2010; Morabito et al., 2010b), disease states (O'Neil and Emeson, 2012; Zhu et al., 2012), pharmacological manipulations (Abbas et al., 2010) or reovirus infections (Hood et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Htr2c RNA editing appears robustly controlled very likely by distinct overlapping mechanisms.
source: Hence, Htr2c RNA editing appears robustly controlled very likely by distinct overlapping mechanisms and Snord115 might only be one of these regulators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed robustness of editing patterns.

claim: Snord115 might only be one of multiple regulators of Htr2c RNA editing.
source: Hence, Htr2c RNA editing appears robustly controlled very likely by distinct overlapping mechanisms and Snord115 might only be one of these regulators.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.
